Migliarini et al. (2026) → Trust formation and revision

FND-155 Safeguard cost trade-offs: Reasoning steps, ensembles,
retrieval grounding and verification improve structure and stability
but cost latency, tokens and energy: budget them, switch them on by
risk, and keep human oversight, especially in agentic use
  Interview question: Q#2.2, Q#9, Q#13

Long et al. (2026) → Verification effort and limits

FND-151 Run-based verification: Verification mostly runs the code: of
166 verification actions 87% checked output and 13% inspected internal
logic; students named 22 decision factors, 11 challenges (the most
common, from 19 of 27, is how candidates are displayed and switched;
14 had not noticed that other candidates exist) and 23 expectations
(15 of 27 want better natural-language interaction)
  Interview question: Q#2.2, Q#10, Q#14

Torun et al. (2026) → Gains and named risks

FND-163 Named risks: Named risks: accountability gap from opaque LLM
decisions (answer: named human reviewers), hallucination, errors
cascading across steps, privacy, hidden API and integration costs, and
resistance, role displacement and deskilling, including shadow
processes outside the tracker
  Interview question: Q#4, Q#10, Q#13, Q#14

Long et al. (2026) → Output problems, felt productivity

FND-149 Felt more productive: Students felt more productive with the
tool: about 30% found the task easy with it, while over 50% found it
difficult without; about 55% rated their own performance bad without
it, and over 55% agree that programming without an assistant is
strenuous
  Interview question: Q#2.3, Q#9

Hassan et al. (2026) → Subgroup effects, seniority

FND-157 Bloat, selective acceptance: Assistants lean towards additive
changes and bloat; the authors cite a Cursor study (more speed at
first, then higher complexity and warnings), seniors accepting fewer
suggestions than juniors, and a survey of about 500 developers who
skip AI for lack of need, inaccuracy, low trust, a wish for control or
missing context
  Interview question: Q#8, Q#9, Q#10, Q#12

Hassan et al. (2026) → Augmentation forms, joint tools

FND-158 Intent-centric SE 3.0: Vision: intent-centric,
conversation-oriented development in which an AI teammate clarifies
intent and drives code creation; code is secondary and hidden by
default, conversations are archived and versioned; stack of
Teammate.next, IDE.next, Compiler.next, Runtime.next and FM.next
  Interview question: Q#2, Q#6

Migliarini et al. (2026) → Prompt-layer engineering

FND-154 Versioned, auditable prompts: Prompts, context bindings,
retrieval scope and checks should be versioned, auditable artefacts,
described by four capability groups (policy and context, prompt
planning, provenance and audit, evaluation and reporting) and a
minimum reporting kit (model and version, decoding, retrieval scope,
cache and access policies)
  Interview question: Q#3, Q#4, Q#7
FND-152 Four recurring problems: Four recurring problems: policy and
project context are not bound at invocation and provenance is too thin
for review; prompt patterns do not transfer across models, versions or
repositories; safeguards add latency, tokens and energy; some risks
need escalation beyond the prompt layer, with no standard thresholds
  Interview question: Q#3, Q#4, Q#13
FND-153 Prompt-layer limits: Prompt-layer controls can constrain
output, scope retrieval, require citations and record provenance, but
cannot remove entrenched representational harms or unintended
memorisation: those need model, data or organisational governance
  Interview question: Q#4, Q#11

Long et al. (2026) → Tool limits, steerability

FND-150 Backtracking patterns: Most interaction paths end at accept or
reject; comment-style prompts were accepted less (43.2%) than code
(48.2%) or context (50.1%) prompts; 'slowly accepted' (retyped)
suggestions were never backtracked, whereas changing earlier code to
fit a suggestion ended in backtracking in 7 of 7 cases
  Interview question: Q#2.1, Q#2.2, Q#7

Hassan et al. (2026) → Tool limits, steerability

FND-156 SE 2.0 limits: Limits of today's AI-assisted SE ('SE 2.0'):
the developer still drives the loop and carries the load of
decomposing, prompting, judging suggestions and debugging; wrong
suggestions can lead into debugging 'rabbit holes'
  Interview question: Q#2.1, Q#2.2, Q#7, Q#10

Hassan et al. (2026) → Needs, taxonomies, teaching prompting

FND-159 Challenges, open questions: Five challenges and 14 open
questions, e.g. speeding human–AI intent alignment ('humans are the
bottleneck, not the AI'), efficient synthesis, edge routing, better SE
knowledge in models and removing the need for prompt engineering
  Interview question: Q#3, Q#7, Q#10, Q#14

Torun et al. (2026) → Agent workflow, evaluation challenges

FND-161 Proposed agent workflow: Proposed flow: end users report in
natural language; agents enhance reports, try to reproduce them,
classify and validate them, and resolve invalid ones without code;
valid bugs go to assigned developers who review LLM patches before
CI/CD deploys
  Interview question: Q#2.1, Q#2.2, Q#6
FND-160 Nine bug-tracking challenges: Manual bug tracking depends on
people reporting, reproducing, triaging and fixing; the paper lists
nine challenges across the workflow, from incomplete reports and hard
reproduction to labour-intensive triage and slow asynchronous
exchanges between end users and developers
  Interview question: Q#6, Q#10

Long et al. (2026) → Tool-dependent edit modes

FND-148 Tool-dependent acceptance: Completion acceptance averaged 49%
for CodeGeeX, 39% for Copilot and 24% for Tabnine; comment and string
completions were accepted least; 12 of 27 used any other feature (9
natural-language-to-code) and 7 of the 15 non-users did not know such
features existed
  Interview question: Q#3, Q#6, Q#9

Kam et al. (2025) → Early-adopter samples

GAP-108 Small early-adopter sample: Small sample of 21 early adopters
with limited diversity (experts with deep AI use were hard to find in
2023); findings may not generalise as adoption spreads and the field
evolves.
  Interview question: Q#1, Q#8, Q#14

Tabarsi et al. (2026) → Early-adopter samples

GAP-117 Homogeneous early adopters: Participants were mostly US-based
White or Asian men with 3+ years of experience; purposive,
self-selected early adopters, so results may skew to more engaged or
experienced users; other groups' experiences may differ.
  Interview question: Q#1

Baumann et al. (2026) → Early-adopter samples

GAP-031 Public early adopters: Early adopters on public repos who opt
in to logging; no proprietary enterprise code, so patterns may differ
(e.g. legacy code); about 16% of sessions come from the tool maker's
own repo.
  Interview question: Q#1, Q#2, Q#5

Tang et al. (2026) → Early-adopter samples

GAP-035 Opt-in early adopters: Developers who use SpecStory or
Entire.io and opt in to public logging: early adopters; weaker agents,
private projects and internal organisational use are
under-represented; a snapshot of a fast-changing practice.
  Interview question: Q#1, Q#2, Q#8

GAP-015 Association, not cause: Cross-sectional adoption data cannot
separate peer influence from homophily; heavier-use weeks read as

quality costs.

GAP-081 Cross-sectional, two firms: Cross-sectional, self-reported
survey (associations, not causes) of self-selected respondents at
GitHub and Microsoft only; the model cannot capture every factor.
  Interview question: Q#1, Q#12

Choudhuri et al. (2026) → Cross-sectional single-firm data

GAP-097 Single-company, self-reported: Cross-sectional and
self-reported (associations, not causation; self-selection); one
company (Microsoft), so results may not transfer to smaller
organisations or open source; frequencies for qualitative themes
deliberately not reported.
  Interview question: Q#1, Q#12

Giray et al. (2026) → Self-selected, self-reported samples

GAP-085 Self-reported global sample: Self-reported, non-probability

recall, social-desirability and self-assessment bias; findings may not
generalise.
  Interview question: Q#1

GAP-075 Self-reported, English, corporate: Self-reported use and
checking (social desirability, participation bias; participants may

  Interview question: Q#1, Q#2, Q#2.2

Stray et al. (2025) → Narrow organisation or enthusiast samples

GAP-089 One public organisation: One public-sector organisation,

firms or other cultures is untested.
  Interview question: Q#1, Q#12

GAP-120 Self-reported convenience sample: Self-reports (survey and

  Interview question: Q#1

Huang et al. (2026) → Narrow organisation or enthusiast samples

GAP-028 AI-positive narrow sample: AI-positive survey sample (99, 98%

only 13 observations.
  Interview question: Q#1, Q#14

Liang et al. (2024) → Narrow organisation or enthusiast samples

GAP-053 Enthusiast sample, dated: Sample drawn from GitHub projects
about AI assistants (Copilot, Tabnine), so mostly enthusiasts; people
not interested in the tools are under-represented; survey run in
January 2023, tools have since changed.
  Interview question: Q#1, Q#8, Q#14

GAP-013 Efficiency, not total: The estimate is an efficiency effect:

productivity effect could be larger.
  Interview question: Q#2.3, Q#9

GAP-010 Saved-time destination: Coding is only one part of a
developer's job, so time saved on coding may not become extra output;

  Interview question: Q#2.3, Q#9

Choudhuri et al. (2026) → Saved-time destination

GAP-099 Saved-time destination: Whether time saved on toil becomes

  Interview question: Q#2.3, Q#9, Q#10

GAP-076 Blind-trust drift: Test whether quality gains and growing
habit lead to blind trust and less security checking (the authors'
hypothesis for future research).
  Interview question: Q#2.2, Q#8, Q#9

Choudhuri et al. (2026) → Trust and role drift over time

GAP-098 Transferability, repeat measurement: Test transferability in
other contexts; re-run the instrument periodically to see whether
tooling improvements shift developer experience; research on goal
maintenance (drift) and steerability (autonomy levels).
  Interview question: Q#8, Q#9, Q#10, Q#14

Stray et al. (2025) → Trust and role drift over time

GAP-091 Workflow evolution, trust: How GenAI shapes developer
workflows over time, especially how teams refine their use and handle
trust, knowledge transfer and workflow integration.
  Interview question: Q#5, Q#8, Q#9, Q#12

Zakharov et al. (2025) → Trust and role drift over time

GAP-072 Role evolution, onboarding: How developers' conceptualisations
of AI evolve over time, and how onboarding strategies shape role
attribution and trust.
  Interview question: Q#5, Q#8, Q#9

GAP-080 Longitudinal trust evolution: Observe developers over longer
periods to see how trust evolves and settles; study automation bias;
estimate maintainability and robustness for small snippets; test how
age, experience, education, project type and culture shape trust.
  Interview question: Q#1, Q#8, Q#9, Q#12

Long et al. (2026) → Learning versus reliance

GAP-149 Learning versus reliance: Productivity and difficulty are
self-reported on short tasks, with no measure of learning or

  Interview question: Q#7, Q#8, Q#9

GAP-048 Learning loop unmeasured: 13 interviews in an exploratory

GAP-113 Learning unmeasured: Learning outcomes were not studied

teaching tools.
  Interview question: Q#7, Q#8, Q#14

Giray et al. (2026) → Expertise redistribution, validation

GAP-088 Expertise redistribution: Longitudinal research on how
expertise is redistributed (problem framing, creation, delegation,
validation, judgement) and how this affects learning and professional
development.
  Interview question: Q#7, Q#8, Q#14

Amalfitano et al. (2026) → Expertise redistribution, validation

GAP-129 Untested expertise claims: Roadmap claims about eroding human
expertise and accountability are not yet tested against practitioners'
accounts.
  Interview question: Q#7, Q#9, Q#14

Huang et al. (2026) → Expertise redistribution, validation

GAP-029 Single-session observation: Each observation was one 45-minute
session, so no longitudinal use or full development cycle.
  Interview question: Q#2, Q#8

Choudhuri et al. (2025) → Expertise redistribution, validation

GAP-082 Longitudinal, GenAI-specific constructs: Use longitudinal data
and control for familiarity and demographics; examine GenAI-specific
constructs such as ease of prompting and tinkering with prompt

  Interview question: Q#6, Q#7, Q#8, Q#9

Nguyen-Duc & Khanna (2024) → Expertise redistribution, validation

GAP-104 Objective, longitudinal validation: Evaluate the task list

established settings to see sustained benefits and challenges; the
authors say they are limited in empirically supporting the value
claims.
  Interview question: Q#8, Q#9

Wu et al. (2026) → Long-term quality outcomes

GAP-060 Long-term quality outcomes: Study the S-IASE model where code

granularity; run more experiments built on it.
  Interview question: Q#9

Watanabe et al. (2026) → Long-term quality outcomes

GAP-135 Acceptance-only success: Acceptance is the only success

still-open PRs are excluded (survival bias), so slow or contested
cases are missing.
  Interview question: Q#2.2, Q#2.3, Q#9

Murphy-Hill et al. (2026) → Long-term quality outcomes

GAP-016 Short horizon: The 16-week window is long enough to show an
early fade but not a long-horizon decline.
  Interview question: Q#8, Q#9

Borg et al. (2026) → Long-term quality outcomes

GAP-018 Short-term only: Only short-term maintainability is observed;

  Interview question: Q#8, Q#9

tests and review, is untested; the case rests on a vision and ten

  Interview question: Q#2.2, Q#14

  Interview question: Q#2, Q#2.2, Q#9, Q#14

Borg et al. (2026) → Hidden code, bloat, practice evidence

GAP-020 Bloat, cognitive debt: Research on when LLM output improves

understanding of AI-generated code), and on knowledge management in
organisations.
  Interview question: Q#9, Q#12, Q#14

Brun et al. (2026) → Hidden code, bloat, practice evidence

GAP-131 No practice evidence: A vision for formal verification with no

and responsibility play out day to day is not examined.
  Interview question: Q#2.2, Q#9, Q#14

Brandebusemeyer et al. (2026) → Weak outcome and load measures

GAP-069 Subjective load measures: Perceived cognitive load,
productivity and satisfaction are individual, experience- and
task-dependent; objective data (physiological, keyboard and mouse) are
still to be analysed.
  Interview question: Q#2.3, Q#9, Q#10

Moreno-Lumbreras et al. (2026) → Weak outcome and load measures

GAP-144 Seven-part agenda: A seven-part agenda: provenance and
code-evolution tracking, intent-based navigation, interactive
regeneration with constraints, parallel exploration without decision
fatigue, continuous regeneration pipelines, sandboxing and safety, and
cognitive load, trust and explainability.
  Interview question: Q#3, Q#4, Q#9, Q#10

Heilman et al. (2026) → Weak outcome and load measures

GAP-012 Narrow outcome measure: PR count captures activity and
efficiency only; satisfaction, performance and communication are
unmeasured; PR complexity is only partly captured (Azure DevOps repos
only).
  Interview question: Q#9, Q#10, Q#12

Baumann et al. (2026) → Weak outcome and load measures

GAP-032 Abandoned sessions missing: Abandoned sessions are missing
(success likely overestimated); line-level attribution can undercount
agent code that survives in changed form; committed lines and prompt
characters only proxy satisfaction and efficiency.
  Interview question: Q#2.3, Q#9, Q#10

Baumann et al. (2026) → Effects and reasons unasked

GAP-034 Pushback reasons hidden: Reasons for pushing back in about
half of turns, and agent use inside companies, are not visible in
session logs.
  Interview question: Q#2.2, Q#9, Q#10

Hao et al. (2024) → Effects and reasons unasked

GAP-040 Effects, reasons unasked: Effects on productivity and quality
are not measured, and the reasons developers share or refine
conversations are inferred from text, not asked.
  Interview question: Q#2.3, Q#7, Q#9

Cui et al. (2026) → Effects and reasons unasked

GAP-009 Code quality effects: A more extensive study of code quality,
since effects look heterogeneous (build success fell at Accenture, no
decline at Microsoft).
  Interview question: Q#2.3, Q#9

Li et al. (2026) → Effects and reasons unasked

GAP-139 Effects, not use: Effect, not use: study how ChatGPT affects
productivity, code quality and defect rates in controlled experiments
with and without it; the paper describes use only and measures no
outcome.
  Interview question: Q#2.3, Q#9

Zakharov et al. (2025) → Effects and reasons unasked

GAP-071 Roles versus outcomes: A short, correlational study with no
outcome measures: whether the roles developers assign to AI change
quality, speed or reliance is untested.
  Interview question: Q#2.3, Q#9, Q#12

Mozannar et al. (2024) → Researcher-set short tasks

GAP-055 Short Python tasks: Time-limited tasks set by the authors,
mostly Python (2 of 21 used C++ or JavaScript); each segment assumed
to hold one state; longer-term costs such as security vulnerabilities
and over-reliance not captured.
  Interview question: Q#8, Q#9, Q#10

Barke et al. (2023) → Researcher-set short tasks

GAP-051 Researcher-set authorship tasks: Tasks were set by the
researchers, not participants' own projects or time pressure, and
covered code authorship only (no refactoring, testing or debugging).
  Interview question: Q#2, Q#6

Chen et al. (2025) → Researcher-set short tasks

GAP-061 Student, timed tasks: Time-limited tasks set by the
researchers and scored by test cases passed; participants all
students; web-based editor, not an enterprise IDE; chat-based
conditions only.
  Interview question: Q#1, Q#2

Chen et al. (2026) → Student samples, short tasks

GAP-022 Students, short tasks: Mostly students with no prior agent
experience, a few pre-defined single tasks, popular languages;
planning and specification with AI are left for future work.
  Interview question: Q#1, Q#2, Q#6

Barke et al. (2023) → Student samples, short tasks

GAP-052 Academic, novice sample: 20 participants skewed to academia;
11 were first-time Copilot users (sometimes over-reliant); other tasks
and languages could change the interactions.
  Interview question: Q#1, Q#8, Q#9

Perry et al. (2023) → Student samples, short tasks

GAP-073 Student sample: Participants were mainly university students,
who may not represent regular users; professional developers may have
stronger security backgrounds and more incentive to test code.
  Interview question: Q#1, Q#2.2, Q#9

Mozannar et al. (2024) → Student samples, short tasks

GAP-057 Value beyond correctness: Find metrics beyond code correctness
that capture the value added for users.
  Interview question: Q#2.3, Q#9

Li et al. (2026) → Shared public chats only

GAP-138 Shared public chats: Only conversations developers chose to
share on public GitHub (English, ChatGPT, May 2023 to June 2024), with
some noise and duplicates: private, company and unshared use, other
tools and later models are not seen, and patterns may have shifted
since.
  Interview question: Q#2, Q#3, Q#8

Hao et al. (2024) → Shared public chats only

GAP-038 Shared chats only: Only conversations developers shared in
GitHub PRs and issues (DevGPT, data up to October 2023); results may
not generalise to other conversations or platforms, and the dataset
misses the last turn of multi-turn conversations. The authors invite
replication on larger or other open-source data.
